note: Story director on the new core (docs/design/director-on-core2.md). Developer data, never shown to a player. Channels, kept-fact kinds and tie rows are open data rows; the code registers one measure per channel operation.

directorMomentFloor.citation: The smallest row of the Holmes and Rahe (1967), The Social Readjustment Rating Scale, Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, Table 3, 'Minor violations of the law', 11 life-change units divided by 100. The 2021 replication rates it 22.14 (Wallace, Cooper, Sel and Russo (2023), PLOS ONE 18(12):e0295943, Table 3 (540 mostly British adults, 2021, marriage fixed at 50)); if the director adopts the 2021 scale, the floor (0.22) and the 0.50 interrupt line change together or not at all.

directorInterruptImpact.citation: Owner ruling on answer 2, October 9, 2026: the scale's anchor event, 'Marriage', 50 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967), so losing a household's only pay takes over the screen.

directorScaleFeeling.citation: Identity: the core's appraised event impulses are already expressed on the life-change scale divided by 100 (src/core2/emotion.ts appraiseEvent).

directorFeelingSignals.citation: The core's appraisal carries an event's size on two signals, mood and stress (src/core2/emotion.ts appraiseEvent); the drives package puts the same life-change share on each (src/core2/modules/health.ts severityImpulse). Averaging the two returns that share.

directorScaleTie.citation: Holmes and Rahe (1967) 'Change in number of arguments with spouse', 35 life-change units divided by 100; the October 8, 2026 story director design caps relationship moments at this row.
directorScaleTie.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967) Social Readjustment Rating Scale

directorScaleCause.citation: Identity: drive strength from the drives package is already trait-weighted on the life-change impulse scale.

directorScaleReentry.citation: Identity: a re-entry adds the pair's importance from before it faded, which is already a sum of moment impacts and standing ties (October 8, 2026 story director design, part 5, rule 1).

directorScaleMoney.citation: Holmes and Rahe (1967) 'Fired at work', 47 life-change units divided by 100, applied to a loss of the household's whole yearly pay.
directorScaleMoney.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967) Social Readjustment Rating Scale

directorScaleHome.citation: Holmes and Rahe (1967) 'Change in residence', 20 life-change units divided by 100.
directorScaleHome.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967) Social Readjustment Rating Scale

directorScaleHealth.citation: The watched person's own death ends the watched life; scale 1 places it at the top of the life-change scale. No direct source for the director's weighting.

directorWeightTieSociability.citation: The October 8, 2026 design's trait tilt at full strength (one quarter), reused for sociability on the tie channel. No direct source. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION, kept as an upper bound (0 is not contradicted). No source gives a weight for sociability on the importance of a tie change; Yap, Anusic and Lucas (2012), Journal of Research in Personality 46(5):477-488, found personality did not consistently moderate reactions to marriage, childbirth, unemployment and widowhood, which argues against a large tilt.

directorWeightMoneyRisk.citation: The October 8, 2026 design's trait tilt at full strength (one quarter), signed so that a person who avoids risk weighs a money loss more. No direct source. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION, kept as an upper bound in size (0 is not contradicted). No study ties risk preference to the weight of a money loss; Yap, Anusic and Lucas (2012) found no consistent Big Five moderation of responses to events, unemployment among them.

directorCostHorizonDays.citation: Average Gregorian month: 146,097 days per 400 years divided by 4,800 months.

directorTieParent.citation: Story director design, part 2, October 8, 2026 calibration (data/content/story-threads.json). Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept; no source ranks this tie against parents and children for story importance, and no measured decay exists for how much a faded tie still matters.

directorTiePartner.citation: Not in the October 8, 2026 calibration, which had no partner row. Scaled from the parent anchor (0.5) by the ratio of a spouse's death to a close family member's death on the same scale: 100 against 63 in Holmes and Rahe (1967), The Social Readjustment Rating Scale, Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, Table 3 gives 0.79; 86.83 against 75.84 in the 2021 replication (Wallace, Cooper, Sel and Russo (2023), PLOS ONE 18(12):e0295943, Table 3 (540 mostly British adults, 2021, marriage fixed at 50)) gives 0.57. Derived, not published; the 1967 ratio is used because every other director row is on the 1967 scale.
directorTiePartner.estimatedFrom: Parent tie 0.5 times the Holmes and Rahe (1967) ratio of 'Death of a spouse' (100) to 'Death of a close family member' (63).

spread.citation: 1967 ratio (0.79) and 2021 replication ratio (0.57) of spouse death to close-family death.

directorTieSharedHome.citation: Story director design, part 2, October 8, 2026 calibration (data/content/story-threads.json). Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept; no source ranks this tie against parents and children for story importance, and no measured decay exists for how much a faded tie still matters.

directorFadingDiscount.citation: Story director design, part 2, October 8, 2026 calibration: fading discounts a pair's moments by up to three quarters. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept; no source ranks this tie against parents and children for story importance, and no measured decay exists for how much a faded tie still matters.

directorFriendHalfLifeDays.citation: About 18 months, the same value P15 uses for closeness between people who are not relatives. Roberts and Dunbar (2015), Managing relationship decay, Human Nature 26(4):426-450: friends' inner-layer retention over 18 months was 69 of 142 (48.6%), an exponential equivalent of 526 days. Long-run check: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37:65-80, 48% of discussion partners and helpers remained after seven years (a 2,415-day half-life that includes contact).
directorFriendHalfLifeDays.estimatedFrom: Roberts and Dunbar (2015) friend inner-layer retention converted to an exponential half-life (526 days); 25 school leavers in transition, no half-life reported in the paper.

spread.citation: Roberts and Dunbar (2015) derived 526 days; Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014) 2,415 days with contact included.

directorKinHalfLifeDays.citation: About 36 months, the same value (1,095 days) P15 uses for relatives. Roberts and Dunbar (2015), Managing relationship decay, Human Nature 26(4):426-450: relatives' inner-layer retention over 18 months was 102 of 145 (70.3%), an exponential equivalent of 1,078 days. Long-run check: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37:65-80 (2,415-day half-life that includes contact).
directorKinHalfLifeDays.estimatedFrom: Roberts and Dunbar (2015) relative inner-layer retention converted to an exponential half-life (1,078 days); 25 school leavers in transition, no half-life reported in the paper.

spread.citation: Roberts and Dunbar (2015) derived 1,078 days; Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014) 2,415 days with contact included.

directorRenewedFading.citation: Labeling only: a contact is labeled a renewal when at least half of the pair's closeness had faded, one half-life. Decides no outcome.

directorAnniversaryHalfDays.citation: Owner answer 7, October 9, 2026: a weight highest on the anniversary that falls smoothly over two weeks either side; it halves every 7 days from the date, with no cut-off. No direct source. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept at the owner's answer (7). No study measures how long grief or recall stays elevated around an anniversary; the one large quantitative study measured mortality in the week of a child's death and was inconclusive (mothers' relative risk 1.46, interval 0.98 to 2.17; Eur J Epidemiol 2015, DOI 10.1007/s10654-015-9989-5).

directorPastChildBorn.citation: A recorded past fact scores the stress scale's 'Gain of a new family member' row, 39 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe (1967), The Social Readjustment Rating Scale, Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, Table 3; the 2021 replication rates it 51.81, Wallace, Cooper, Sel and Russo (2023), PLOS ONE 18(12):e0295943, Table 3 (540 mostly British adults, 2021, marriage fixed at 50)). The 1967 values are a lower bound; they are kept so every director row sits on one scale.

directorPastPartner.citation: A recorded past fact scores the stress scale's 'Marriage' row, 50 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe (1967), The Social Readjustment Rating Scale, Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, Table 3; the 2021 replication rates it 50, Wallace, Cooper, Sel and Russo (2023), PLOS ONE 18(12):e0295943, Table 3 (540 mostly British adults, 2021, marriage fixed at 50)). The 1967 values are a lower bound; they are kept so every director row sits on one scale.

directorMemoryRecentDays.citation: No study sets how long a person keeps every moment in full. A season (91 days) keeps the recent past whole for scenes, callbacks and the journal; older moments keep only the strongest by hindsight. Checked by a watched person's stored moments staying about the same size across a year (P15 two-level population).

directorMemoryKeptMoments.citation: No study sets how many older moments a person keeps one by one. Two a month over a year, matching the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's twelve-month window (Holmes and Rahe 1967); the rest stay as monthly summaries and as each pair's summed impact. Checked by stored moments staying about the same size across a year.

directorFilingImpact.citation: Filing to run for office, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Outstanding personal achievement', 28 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967), the same scale the director uses for every life event.

directorKinMovedImpact.citation: Someone close moving away, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Son or daughter leaving home', 29 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967), reaching those tied to the movers by how much they matter to them.

directorEvictionImpact.citation: Losing one's home to eviction, sized like losing one's job (the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Fired at work', 47 life-change units divided by 100; its nearest item, 'Foreclosure of mortgage or loan', 30, understates it per Desmond and Kimbro 2015, Social Forces 94(1):295-324), the same size the drives engine gives an eviction.
directorEvictionImpact.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967); Desmond and Kimbro (2015); spread 0.3 to 0.47

directorHomePurchaseImpact.citation: Buying a home, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Mortgage over $10,000', 31 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967).

directorBusinessFoundedImpact.citation: Starting a business, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Business readjustment', 39 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967).

directorBirthImpact.citation: A child born into the family, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Gain of new family member', 39 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967), reaching the parents fully and others tied to them by how much they matter.

directorElectionWonImpact.citation: Winning an election, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Change to a different line of work', 36 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967): the office becomes the winner's work.

directorElectionLostImpact.citation: Losing an election, sized as the run it ends: the filing that began it ('Outstanding personal achievement', 28 life-change units divided by 100, Holmes and Rahe 1967). The scale has no item for losing a contest.

directorTookOfficeImpact.citation: Taking office, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Change in responsibilities at work', 29 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967).

directorBodyVoteImpact.citation: A member's vote on a bill, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Change in work hours or conditions', 20 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967).

directorBusinessClosedImpact.citation: A business closing, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Business readjustment', 39 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967), as its founding is.

directorTownHallHostImpact.citation: Holding a town hall, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Change in work hours or conditions', 20 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967).

directorTownHallImpact.citation: Going to a town hall, sized as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Change in social activities', 18 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967).

directorMarriedImpact.citation: Marrying, the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's anchor item 'Marriage', 50 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967), as the director's past partnership moment is.

interruptStop.citation: The story director's stored moment: its impact, measured from the change on each channel and sized by the person's traits, is at or over the interrupt line, the Holmes and Rahe (1967) marriage anchor of 50 life-change units divided by 100 (owner ruling, October 9, 2026; CTO ruling on at-or-over, October 10, 2026).
